svg.title: The spectrogram — okfy algorithm explainer
svg.desc: How the rolling mel spectrogram is drawn. Three sources feed one renderer: the assistant's speech through an analyser of fftSize 2048 and smoothing 0.5, drawn on the commentary bubble; an audio clip's preview through the same settings, drawn on the player's framed canvas; and the microphone through fftSize 1024 and smoothing 0.4, drawn on the listening bubble. The fast Fourier transform is the browser's analyser, which reports one decibel value per frequency bin; what the tool adds is the mel pooling, the decibel scale, the colour ramp and the rolling history. One animation frame reads the analyser's spectrum, pools it into forty-eight mel bands in decibels, turns each band into a colour and writes a one-pixel-wide column at the right edge of an offscreen history canvas, then shifts the history one pixel left and blits it to the visible canvas at device-pixel size. The filterbank spreads fifty points, one more than the band count plus one, evenly on the mel scale between zero hertz and the top of the range, capped at the Nyquist frequency, and maps each point back to hertz. Band m is a triangle that rises from point m, peaks at point m plus one and falls to point m plus two, so neighbouring bands overlap. Because the mel scale is nearly linear at the bottom and compresses at the top, the triangles widen as the frequency rises, so the low frequencies, where vowels and formants live, get proportionally more bands. A band's energy is the weighted sum of its frequency bins as power, written in decibels, mapped onto a seventy-decibel window from minus ninety-five to minus twenty-five, raised to the power 0.7 so quiet detail still shows, and mixed from the panel's own dark blue up to the accent colour for loud bands. Band zero, the lowest frequency, is drawn at the bottom, so pitch reads up the column while time runs left to right. The history is an offscreen canvas: each frame bakes the newest column onto its right edge, shifts the whole history one pixel left using copy compositing, which also clears the freed column so the newest column always lands on empty pixels, and blits the result to the visible canvas. A fresh clip or utterance clears the history, so its spectrogram rolls in from an empty field rather than splicing onto the last one. A snapshot copies the history into a canvas of its own, which is what keeps a spectrogram in a bubble after playback has ended and lets it be redrawn when the bubble re-renders. Only audio draws this view, because a video plays in a plain media element with the browser's own controls. The view is computed live from the analyser, so it costs one pooled spectrum per frame and never per sample, while the clip's bytes are bounded separately: a clip up to 256 mebibytes is read whole, one small enough to decode within 32 mebibytes is decoded for grain-accurate scrubbing, and above that a local clip streams from its object URL into the same analyser.
svg.text: A rolling mel view of the live audio graph, drawn from one analyser frame
An AnalyserNode each, and the same frame for all three
The FFT is the browser's analyser: it reports one decibel value per frequency bin. The mel pooling,
the decibel scale, the colour ramp and the rolling history are the tool's, and one frame draws them all.
One animation frame, about sixty times a second
The newest column is one pixel wide and one band tall, written at the right edge of an offscreen
history canvas. The history is then shifted one pixel to the left and blitted to the visible canvas,
sized in device pixels so the trace stays crisp on a high-density screen.
A band's height is the canvas height divided by 48, and band 0 is drawn at the bottom.
Points spaced on the mel scale, so the bands widen as they rise
The points are spread evenly in mel, not in hertz, so each band's triangle is wider than the one below it.
Band m rises from point m, peaks at m + 1 and falls to m + 2, so neighbouring bands overlap; the whole set
is built for the analyser's own fftSize and sample rate, and capped at the Nyquist frequency.
4 · One column, from decibels to colour
Forty-eight bands, each one a tint between two colours
A band's energy is the weighted sum of its bins as power, written in decibels.
The window is 70 dB wide, and the 0.7 power lifts quiet detail so a soft phoneme still shows.
A band below the window is the panel colour itself; one at the top is the accent.
Band 0, the lowest frequency, sits at the bottom, so pitch reads up the column.
In the real view each band is 1 px tall and a column of 48 is one frame of the history.
Bake the newest column, shift one pixel, blit
a fresh clip clears the history, so the trace rolls in from the right
Each frame bakes the newest column onto the right edge of
the offscreen history, shifts it one pixel left, and blits it
to the visible canvas, sized in device pixels.
The shift uses copy compositing, which clears the freed
column, so the newest column lands on empty pixels.
A snapshot copies the history into its own canvas, so the
spectrogram stays in a bubble after playback has ended and
is redrawn whenever the bubble is re-rendered.
Only audio draws this view: a video plays in a plain media element with the browser's own controls.
It is computed live from the analyser — one pooled spectrum per frame, never per sample — so it costs the
same for a long clip as for a short one.
